assumptions: Shipper shares are shares of the parcels delivered on a mean weekday; the generator draws the day's total (3,500 with standard deviation 350, times the weekday multiplier and the seasonal factor) and splits it by these shares, keeping the shipper mix the same all year.
The shipper list reproduces the fixed totals: 58.1% small, 30.2% medium, 11.7% large parcels and 32.1% business recipients.
business_share is the share of a shipper's parcels that go to business recipients; it is 0 for consumer shippers, 1 for business shippers and in between for mixed shippers.

A shipper's business parcels are spread across its listed zones in proportion to each zone's share of daily parcels; consumer parcels then fill each zone up to its fixed share, so the zone totals stay as in the company profile.

With these zone lists, business recipients take this share of each zone's parcels: Z01 35%, Z02 39%, Z03 42%, Z04 31%, Z05 22%, Z06 25%, Z07 17%, Z08 24%, Z09 33%, Z10 38%, Z11 30%, Z12 37%, Z13 16%, Z14 37%.

Overnight linehaul trailers reach the hub between 02:00 and 05:30, morning injections are dropped by the shipper's own vans between 05:30 and 07:30, and midday injections arrive between 12:00 and 13:30.
Parcels that reach the hub before 08:00 (overnight linehaul and morning injection) can go out in either wave; midday injections can only go out in the 15:00-21:00 wave of the day they arrive.

Only midday-injection shippers sell same-day delivery; a midday shipper's next-day parcels (orders registered after 11:00 the day before) travel with its next midday drop and are delivered in the afternoon-evening wave.

Only orders registered before 11:00 can be same-day, and 28.2% of the day's orders are registered before 11:00, so no shipper's same_day_share exceeds that; the generator marks a pre-11:00 order as same-day with probability same_day_share / 0.282 and every order registered from 11:00 onwards as next-day.
Same-day parcels are about 5.2% of all parcels, roughly 180 on a mean weekday.

Business parcels from overnight and morning arrivals always go in the morning wave; business parcels from midday shippers go in the afternoon-evening wave and must be delivered before the recipient closes.

The hourly registration curve mixes consumer online shopping (steady from mid-morning, a dip over the Spanish lunch hours 14:00-16:00 and the main peak at 21:00-22:00 after dinner) with business orders placed in office hours; the 10:00-10:59 peak reflects shippers pushing orders in before the 11:00 same-day cut-off, and the drop at 11:00 follows from it.

Monday is the busiest day because orders placed on Saturday afternoon and Sunday are delivered on Monday; Friday is the quietest weekday because online orders fall off towards the end of the week and shops and businesses avoid restocking just before the weekend; the Monday to Friday multipliers average exactly 1.0 and Saturday is 1,050 / 3,500 = 0.30.
On Saturday most offices, factories and clinics are closed, so the generator only creates business parcels for shops and pharmacies and scales the consumer shippers up to keep the 1,050 total.

consumer_window_choice applies to consumer parcels that are at the hub before 08:00 (52.6% of all parcels); same-day and other midday-injection consumer parcels always go in the afternoon-evening wave.
Across all consumer parcels this gives about 48% in the morning wave and 52% in the afternoon-evening wave; across all parcels about 60% go in the morning wave and 40% in the afternoon-evening wave.

Consumers who pick a specific slot choose one of three 120-minute slots per wave (08-10, 10-12, 12-14 or 15-17, 17-19, 19-21); the rest accept any time in the wave and get their 120-minute window when the routes are planned; business recipients do not pick a slot and get a window inside their opening hours.

Zone difficulty: high for Z01 Ciutat Vella, Z06 Gràcia and Z07 Horta-Guinardó (narrow or pedestrian streets, steep slopes, old buildings without lifts or concierges); medium for Z02, Z03, Z05, Z08, Z09 and Z10; low for Z04, Z11, Z12, Z13 and Z14.

The failed-first-attempt probabilities are for the morning wave; the evening factor applies only to consumer recipients, because more people are at home after work; business recipients keep their base probability, and the route planner never schedules a business stop outside its opening hours.
With this demand mix, the expected first-attempt failure is 10.1% for consumer parcels, 3.5% for business parcels and 8.0% overall, which meets the 92% first-attempt success target.

Parcels per stop is the distribution of stops, not of parcels; parcels at a multi-parcel stop normally belong to the same shipper and order; a '4+' stop gets 4 parcels plus a geometric extra with a mean of 0.4 for consumers and 1.5 for businesses.
This gives on average 1.19 parcels per consumer stop, 2.30 per business stop and 1.41 overall, or about 2,480 stops on a mean weekday.
Shop hours follow the usual Barcelona split day for independent shops; chain stores in shopping centres open longer but accept deliveries only in the same hours.
Office hours assume a staffed reception with a lunch hour; many offices close at 15:00 on Fridays and in July and August, which the generator may ignore.
Industry hours cover the goods-in docks of factories, warehouses and garages, closed over a long lunch break.
Healthcare hours cover pharmacies (many in Barcelona open without a break) and hospital goods-in docks; dental and physiotherapy clinics are treated the same way.

Healthcare shippers carry ambient goods only (over-the-counter medicines, parapharmacy and medical consumables); there are no cold-chain or controlled medicines and no prescription medicines to consumers.
All shipper names are invented for this simulation and do not refer to real companies.
